summaries.example: Imagine a dog in two pictures: in one picture it is a puppy, and in the other it is old and gray. We normally say it is the same dog, even though it looks different. A philosopher who studies relative identity might say the two pictures show the same dog but different stages or objects in time. This helps explain how something can change while still being called the same kind of thing.
summaries.summary: Identity is about sameness. The standard view treats identity as absolute: if two things are identical, they cannot differ in any respect. But many puzzles make this difficult. A dog changes as it grows, a ship may have all its parts replaced, and a statue may occupy the same space as the clay that makes it. Relative identity is the view that two things can be the same F—for example, the same dog—but different Gs—for example, different temporary objects. Some philosophers accept this as a useful way to understand change and other puzzles. Others think there is also absolute identity, or that the puzzles should be solved in different ways. The entry explains both the appeal and the difficulties of these views.
key_ideas: The usual view says that identity is absolute: a thing is either the same as another thing or it is not.
Relative identity says that sameness can depend on the kind of thing being counted, such as a dog, a statue, or a piece of clay.
Changes can make identity puzzling. A dog grows, a ship gets new parts, and clay can be shaped into different statues.
Philosophers disagree about whether relative identity solves these puzzles or creates new ones.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use words like “same,” “different,” and “one” every day. Thinking carefully about them helps us understand change, counting, objects, and names. These puzzles also show that ordinary language can hide difficult questions. Studying different answers teaches us how philosophers test ideas instead of quickly choosing one answer.

important_terms.definition: A question about what makes something the very same thing, rather than merely similar to it.
The idea that two things can be the same kind of thing but not the same thing in every way.
The rule that if two things are truly identical, they cannot differ in any property.
A hard puzzle that seems to lead from reasonable ideas to a strange result.

questions_to_think_about: If a bicycle gets every part replaced, is it still the same bicycle?
Can two pictures show the same dog even though the dog looks different in each one?
Is being the same kind of thing enough to mean being exactly the same thing?
When we count objects, does it matter what kind of objects we are counting?

summaries.example: Suppose a wooden ship is repaired plank by plank until none of its original planks remain. The old planks are then used to build a second ship. Which ship is the original? One answer favors the continuously repaired ship because it has a stronger history of spatial and temporal continuity. Another favors the ship made from the original material. The case suggests that different criteria of identity—continuity, material, or structure—can conflict. Relative identity may describe the ships as the same ship in one respect but different collections of planks in another, though the entry argues that this alone does not fully settle the puzzle.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether identity is an unrestricted relation or whether it is relative to a kind or sortal. On the standard account, identity is an equivalence relation governed by Leibniz’s Law: identicals cannot differ in any respect. This view is powerful, but it faces persistent puzzles. Change seems to involve incompatible properties; a body and a part of it may appear to occupy the same place after amputation; many overlapping parts may each seem to be a dog; a statue and its clay may have different histories and modal properties; and the Ship of Theseus produces competing claims based on continuity and material. Church’s paradox raises related problems about belief and names, while the theological paradox concerns apparently conflicting claims about persons and God. Relative identity proposes that things can be the same F but different Gs. The weak version accepts some relative identity relations while retaining absolute identity. It can model young and old stages as the same dog, or different statues as the same clay. Yet the theory must restrict Leibniz’s Law carefully: if every relative identity relation preserved every property, relative identity would collapse into absolute identity or become inconsistent. The entry also distinguishes genuine sortal-relative identity from ordinary similarity relations, such as having the same color. Finally, it argues that the fact that objects are indistinguishable in one language but distinguishable in a richer language is a model-theoretic phenomenon, not by itself evidence that identity is relative.
key_ideas: The standard account formalizes identity through reflexivity and Leibniz’s Law; symmetry and transitivity follow from these principles.
Identity puzzles arise when an object changes, when parts and wholes overlap, when material constitutes an object, or when names are used in belief reports.
Relative identity allows sameness to be sortal-relative: objects may be the same dog, statue, or piece of clay while differing under another category.
The weak relative-identity view keeps absolute identity while allowing some ordinary identity relations to be relative and to preserve only restricted properties.
Relative identity can offer simple treatments of change, constitution, and some belief puzzles, but it must explain why its relations count as identity rather than mere similarity.
The entry ultimately argues that language-relative indiscernibility does not by itself disprove absolute identity; quotient structures provide one way to recover absolute identity.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects metaphysics, logic, language, and theories of objects. It asks whether “same” has one fundamental meaning or whether sameness depends on what kind of thing is being counted. The answer shapes how we understand persistence through time, material constitution, possible worlds, names, and formal theories. The entry does not present the debate as settled: relative identity illuminates several problems, but its status as a genuine theory of identity and its relation to absolute identity remain contested.

important_terms.definition: The standard logical view that identity is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and obeys Leibniz’s Law.
The principle that identical objects share every property expressible in the relevant language.
A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, such as being the same size or belonging to the same equivalence class.
The claim that x and y can be the same F while being different Gs.
The relation between a material object and an object made from it, such as clay and a statue.
A term whose reference does not vary across times or possible worlds, in the standard sense.
The view that an object extends through time by having different temporal stages or parts.
The claim that identity is the same no matter how rich or limited the descriptive language is.

questions_to_think_about: Does the Ship of Theseus show that identity is indeterminate, or that different criteria are being confused?
If two objects are the same F but differ in some properties, which properties should the relation preserve?
Can constitution be identity without rejecting the necessity of identity?
Does a language’s inability to distinguish two objects show that they are identical, or only that the language is limited?
Should a successful theory explain ordinary identity judgments, preserve logical principles, or minimize the number of objects?

summaries.example: A school makes a clay figure on Monday. On Tuesday, the figure is squashed into a ball and the same clay is used to make a new figure. It is tempting to say that the clay is the same, but the first figure is gone and the second figure is new. If the clay and the first figure were exactly identical, then anything true of one should be true of the other, including when it exists. Relative identity offers a possible description: the two figures are different statues, while the clay is the same piece of clay through the changes.
summaries.summary: The entry studies a disagreement about what “same” means. The standard view says identity is absolute. It is reflexive—everything is the same as itself—and it follows Leibniz’s Law, which says identical things cannot differ in any property. It also treats identity as necessary: if two rigidly named objects are identical, they could not have been distinct. However, many puzzles challenge how easily these rules fit ordinary judgments. A dog can be young in one picture and old in another while remaining the same dog. A piece of clay can first be a statue, then a ball, and later another statue. A ship can be repaired with new parts while its original parts are assembled elsewhere. These cases suggest that different ways of tracking an object—its kind, material, history, or parts—can come apart. Relative identity says that two things can be the same F but different Gs. For example, different statues might be the same piece of clay. Some philosophers use this idea while keeping absolute identity; others reject absolute identity altogether. The entry explains that the view must be carefully limited. If relative identity preserved every property, it would behave like absolute identity, but if it preserved too few properties, it might be only similarity. The debate therefore concerns both logic and how we organize objects into kinds.
key_ideas: The standard account treats identity as absolute and says identical objects must match in every respect.
Everyday cases of change create pressure for this account: a growing dog changes, and a repaired ship may lose all its original parts.
Relative identity claims that two objects may be the same under one sortal but different under another.
The clay-and-statue puzzle asks whether constitution is identity or whether two physical objects can share one place.
The Ship of Theseus shows that material replacement and continuous repair can give competing answers about which ship is original.
Relative identity may help with several puzzles, but it must explain which differences are allowed and why this is identity rather than similarity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Questions about identity appear in ordinary life whenever something changes or gets rebuilt. They also matter in science, law, language, and metaphysics because we often need to decide whether something is one object or several. The debate shows why a simple word such as “same” can support several possible standards. Comparing the theories helps us see both the strengths of common sense and the hidden assumptions behind it.

important_terms.definition: Being exactly one thing and not another, according to the usual philosophical account.
Being the same item under one category but not under another category.
A rule saying that identical things cannot differ in any property.
A reasoning problem in which plausible steps seem to produce an unacceptable conclusion.
A category used to count things, such as “dog,” “ship,” or “statue.”
The material relationship between something and what it is made from.
A relation that has sameness-like features: each thing relates to itself, the relation goes both ways, and it links through chains.
A theory that explains an object as having different parts or stages at different times.

questions_to_think_about: When a person changes greatly, what makes the person remain the same?
Are the repaired ship and the ship made from its old planks both good candidates for being the original?
If two things are the same dog but different physical objects, what kinds of properties should they share?
Is being the same color an example of relative identity or only similarity?
What might a philosopher gain by counting clay and statues differently?
